claim: Approximately 70% of KRAS-positive colorectal cancers (CRCs) have a CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP) characterized by aberrant DNA hypermethylation and transcriptional silencing of many genes.
source: Approximately 70% of KRAS-positive colorectal cancers (CRCs) have a CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP) characterized by aberrant DNA hypermethylation and transcriptional silencing of many genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and is stated as a known fact in the abstract.

claim: The tumor suppressors p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A are encoded by the INK4-ARF locus and are among the CIMP genes.
source: Among the CIMP genes are the tumor suppressors p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A, encoded by the INK4-ARF locus.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the INK4-ARF locus and CIMP genes.

claim: ZNF304 is a zinc-finger DNA-binding protein identified as the pivotal factor required for INK4-ARF silencing and CIMP in CRCs containing activated KRAS.
source: In this study, we perform an RNA interference screen and identify ZNF304, a zinc-finger DNA-binding protein, as the pivotal factor required for INK4-ARF silencing and CIMP in CRCs containing activated KRAS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNAi screen data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In KRAS-positive human CRC cell lines and tumors, ZNF304 is bound at the promoters of INK4-ARF and other CIMP genes.
source: In KRAS-positive human CRC cell lines and tumors, ZNF304 is bound at the promoters of INK4-ARF and other CIMP genes.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figures 2D, 3I, and 6B,D.

claim: Promoter-bound ZNF304 recruits a corepressor complex that includes the DNA methyltransferase DNMT1, resulting in DNA hypermethylation and transcriptional silencing.
source: Promoter-bound ZNF304 recruits a corepressor complex that includes the DNA methyltransferase DNMT1, resulting in DNA hypermethylation and transcriptional silencing.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data (Figure 2D) and bisulfite sequencing data (Figure 2E) showing DNMT1 binding and DNA methylation.

claim: KRAS promotes silencing through upregulation of ZNF304, which drives DNA binding.
source: KRAS promotes silencing through upregulation of ZNF304, which drives DNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that KRAS knockdown reduces ZNF304 protein levels (Figure 3E) and ZNF304 binding to promoters (Figure 3B).

claim: ZNF304 directs transcriptional silencing of INK4-ARF in human embryonic stem cells.
source: Finally, we show that ZNF304 also directs transcriptional silencing of INK4-ARF in human embryonic stem cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7 showing ZNF304 binding and effects of ZNF304 knockdown in H9 hESCs.

claim: CRCs can be categorized into three distinct subclasses based on their epigenetic and genetic profiles: CIMP-1 (CIMP-high), CIMP-2 (CIMP-low), and CIMP-negative.
source: In fact, CRCs can be categorized into three distinct subclasses based on their epigenetic and genetic profiles: CIMP-1 (also called CIMP-high), characterized by intense methylation of multiple genes, microsatellite instability and BRAF mutations; CIMP-2 (also called CIMP-low), typified by methylation of a more limited group of genes and mutation in KRAS; and CIMP-negative, distinguished by infrequent methylation and p53 mutation (Yagi et al., 2010; Kaneda and Yagi, 2011).
evidence: This classification is supported by citations to published literature (Yagi et al., 2010; Kaneda and Yagi, 2011).

claim: INK4-ARF is transcriptionally silenced in 30–45% of all CRCs and in 70% of CRCs that harbor an activating KRAS mutation.
source: For example, INK4-ARF is transcriptionally silenced in 30–45% of all CRCs and in 70% of CRCs that harbor an activating KRAS mutation (Burri et al., 2001; Dominguez et al., 2003; Lind et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Burri et al., 2001; Dominguez et al., 2003; Lind et al., 2004).

claim: The INK4-ARF locus is silenced in embryonic, fetal, and adult stem cells, but in more differentiated cells, it becomes poised for expression and increasingly responsive to aberrant mitogenic signals.
source: For example, INK4-ARF is silenced in embryonic, fetal, and adult stem cells, but in more differentiated cells, it becomes poised for expression and increasingly responsive to aberrant mitogenic signals such as those elicited by activated oncogenes (reviewed in Sherr, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article (Sherr, 2012).

claim: Expression of INK4-ARF limits stem cell self-renewal.
source: Expression of INK4-ARF limits stem cell self-renewal, suggesting that coordinated INK4-ARF expression may normally act to restrict stem cell numbers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The INK4-ARF locus has been shown to be a barrier for reprogramming.
source: Accordingly, the INK4-ARF locus has been shown to be a barrier for reprogramming (Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2009.

claim: In actively growing human diploid fibroblasts, the INK4A-ARF locus is silenced by histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) directed by Polycomb group proteins.
source: In actively growing human diploid fibroblasts, the INK4A-ARF locus is silenced by histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) directed by Polycomb group proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations (Jacobs et al., 1999; Bracken et al., 2007; Kotake et al., 2007).

claim: When cells are exposed to cellular stress, such as oncogenic signals, the H3K27me3 mark on the INK4A-ARF locus is decreased, resulting in expression of INK4A-ARF genes.
source: When such cells are exposed to cellular stress, such as oncogenic signals, the H3K27me3 mark on the locus is decreased, resulting in expression of INK4A-ARF genes (Jacobs et al., 1999; Bracken et al., 2007; Kotake et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Jacobs et al., 1999; Bracken et al., 2007; Kotake et al., 2007).

claim: Transcriptional activation of INK4A-ARF is due, at least in part, to upregulation of the H3K27 demethylase JMJD3, which removes H3K27me3 from INK4A-ARF.
source: Transcriptional activation is due, at least in part, to upregulation of the H3K27 demethylase JMJD3, which removes H3K27me3 from INK4A-ARF (Agger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Agger et al., 2009.

claim: A p14ARF-BlastR reporter construct was stably transduced into DLD-1 cells, and cells in which the reporter gene had been silenced were selected.
source: This p14ARF-BlastR reporter construct was stably transduced into DLD-1 cells, a human CRC cell line in which endogenous p14ARF is transcriptionally silenced (Zheng et al., 2000; Figure 1B). We selected cells in which the reporter gene had been silenced, as evidenced by acquisition of blasticidin resistance (Figure 1C), transcriptional derepression (Figure 1B), and decreased DNA hypermethylation (Figure 1D) following treatment with the DNA methyltransferase inhibitor 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B, 1C, and 1D.

claim: Treatment with 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine resulted in transcriptional derepression of the p14ARF-BlastR reporter in DLD-1 cells.
source: We selected cells in which the reporter gene had been silenced, as evidenced by acquisition of blasticidin resistance (Figure 1C), transcriptional derepression (Figure 1B), and decreased DNA hypermethylation (Figure 1D) following treatment with the DNA methyltransferase inhibitor 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A genome-wide human shRNA library comprising ∼62,400 shRNAs was used to transduce the DLD-1/p14ARF-BlastR reporter cell line.
source: A genome-wide human small hairpin (shRNA) library (Silva et al., 2005) comprising ∼62,400 shRNAs was divided into 10 pools, which were packaged into retrovirus particles and used to stably transduce the DLD-1/p14ARF-BlastR reporter cell line.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the RNAi screen.

claim: Eight genes were identified from the RNAi screen that, following shRNA-mediated knockdown, resulted in derepression of endogenous p14ARF.
source: Using this approach, we identified eight genes that, following shRNA-mediated knockdown, resulted in derepression of endogenous p14ARF (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ZNF304 is a member of the KRAB domain protein family.
source: Therefore, we elected to focus on ZNF304, a zinc finger DNA-binding protein that contains a KRAB repressor domain (Sabater et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sabater et al., 2002.

claim: Knockdown of ZNF304 in DLD-1 cells derepressed p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A.
source: The qRT-PCR and immunoblot results of Figure 2A,B show that in addition to p14ARF, knockdown of ZNF304 derepressed p15INK4B and p16INK4A, which are also transcriptionally silenced in DLD-1 cells (Zheng et al., 2000; Ishiguro et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2A and immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: KRAB domain proteins function by recruiting a corepressor complex that includes the scaffolding protein KAP1 and the histone methyltransferase SETDB1.
source: KRAB domain proteins function by recruiting a corepressor complex that includes the scaffolding protein KAP1 and the histone methyltransferase SETDB1 (Iyengar and Farnham, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Iyengar and Farnham, 2011.

claim: Knockdown of KAP1 or SETDB1 resulted in derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A in DLD-1 cells.
source: Knockdown of KAP1 or SETDB1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) resulted in derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A were substantially derepressed following knockdown of DNMT1 but not DNMT3A or DNMT3B.
source: p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A were also substantially derepressed following knockdown of DNMT1 but not the other DNA methyltransferases, DNMT3A, or DNMT3B (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 were bound to the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters in DLD-1 cells.
source: The chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay of Figure 2D shows that ZNF304, as well as KAP1, SETDB1 and DNMT1, were bound to the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters in DLD-1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Knockdown of ZNF304 substantially decreased binding of KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 to the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters.
source: Notably, knockdown of ZNF304 substantially decreased binding of KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Knockdown of ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, or DNMT1 decreased p14ARF promoter hypermethylation.
source: Knockdown of ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1 or DNMT1 also decreased p14ARF promoter hypermethylation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of ZNF304 in DLD-1 cells significantly suppressed tumor growth in mouse xenografts.
source: Consistent with this prediction, Figure 2F shows that shRNA-mediated knockdown of ZNF304 in DLD-1 cells significantly suppressed tumor growth in mouse xenografts.
evidence: This is supported by tumor formation assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of DNMT1 suppressed tumor growth in mouse xenografts.
source: shRNA-mediated knockdown of DNMT1 similarly suppressed tumor growth, consistent with previous results (Morita et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by tumor formation assay data shown in Figure 2F and a citation to Morita et al., 2013.

claim: DLD-1 cells contain an activated KRAS(G13D) mutation.
source: DLD-1 cells contain an activated KRAS(G13D) mutation and we therefore investigated the relationship between KRAS and silencing of INK4-ARF.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of the DLD-1 cell line.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of KRAS in DLD-1 cells resulted in derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4A, and p16INK4B.
source: shRNA-mediated knockdown of KRAS in DLD-1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) resulted in derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4A, and p16INK4B (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of KRAS substantially reduced binding of ZNF304 and its corepressors to the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters.
source: shRNA-mediated knockdown of KRAS in DLD-1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) resulted in derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4A, and p16INK4B (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and substantially reduced binding of ZNF304 and its corepressors to all three promoters (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment with manumycin A resulted in derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A in DLD-1 cells.
source: Similarly, treatment with manumycin A, a RAS farnesyltransferase inhibitor (Hara et al., 1993), also resulted in derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment with manumycin A reduced binding of ZNF304 and its corepressors to the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters.
source: Similarly, treatment with manumycin A, a RAS farnesyltransferase inhibitor (Hara et al., 1993), also resulted in derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A (Figure 3C) and reduced binding of ZNF304 and its corepressors to the three promoters (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of KRAS markedly reduced ZNF304 protein levels.
source: Notably, shRNA-mediated knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of KRAS markedly reduced ZNF304 protein levels (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Addition of the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 or PI-103 derepressed p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A and reduced ZNF304 levels.
source: Likewise, addition of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor LY294002 (Vlahos et al., 1994) or PI-103, which blocks the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway downstream of activated KRAS (Hayakawa et al., 2006), also derepressed p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A and reduced ZNF304 levels (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Following shRNA-mediated knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of KRAS, ZNF304 mRNA levels were not significantly affected.
source: By contrast, following shRNA-mediated knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of KRAS, ZNF304 mRNA levels were not significantly affected (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Upregulation of ZNF304 by activated KRAS is predominantly post-transcriptional.
source: Thus, upregulation of ZNF304 by activated KRAS is predominantly post-transcriptional.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that KRAS affects ZNF304 protein but not mRNA levels.

claim: The reduction of ZNF304 protein levels following KRAS inhibition could be counteracted by proteasome inhibition.
source: Consistent with this idea, the reduction of ZNF304 protein levels following KRAS inhibition could be counteracted by proteasome inhibition (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: In HCT116 and HCT15 CRC cell lines, ZNF304 and its corepressors were associated with the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters.
source: In HCT116 and HCT15 CRC cell lines, in which INK4-ARF is transcriptionally silenced (Yagi et al., 2010), ZNF304 and its corepressors were associated with the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of ZNF304 or KRAS or treatment with manumycin A derepressed p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A expression in HCT116 and HCT15 cells.
source: Moreover, shRNA-mediated knockdown of ZNF304 or KRAS (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B) or treatment with manumycin A (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C) derepressed p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A expression.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,C.

claim: ZNF304 was substantially enriched at the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters in KRAS-positive human CRC tumor samples relative to adjacent normal colon.
source: Figure 3I shows that ZNF304 was substantially enriched at the three promoters in CRC tumor samples relative to adjacent normal colon.
evidence: This is supported by PAT-ChIP data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Bisulfite sequencing analysis confirmed p14ARF promoter hypermethylation in KRAS-positive CRC tumors but not in matched normal colon.
source: Bisulfite sequencing analysis confirmed p14ARF promoter hypermethylation in the KRAS-positive CRC tumors but not in the matched normal colon (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: USP28 is a nuclear-localized deubiquitinase.
source: Another factor isolated in our primary RNAi screen was USP28 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), a nuclear-localized deubiquitinase (Popov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Popov et al., 2007.

claim: Knockdown of USP28 in DLD-1 cells substantially reduced ZNF304 protein but not mRNA levels.
source: Similar to the results with KRAS, knockdown of USP28 in DLD-1 cells substantially reduced ZNF304 protein (Figure 4A) but not mRNA (Figure 4B) levels.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4A and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4B.

claim: USP28 and ZNF304 were physically associated.
source: The co-immunoprecipitation experiment of Figure 4C shows that USP28 and ZNF304 were physically associated.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Co-transfection of DLD-1 cells with wild-type USP28, but not a catalytically inactive USP28(C171A) mutant, reduced ubiquitination of ZNF304.
source: Moreover, co-transfection of DLD-1 cells with wild-type USP28, but not a catalytically inactive USP28(C171A) mutant (Popov et al., 2007), reduced ubiquitination of ZNF304 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by HA-ubiquitination pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of KRAS led to reduced levels of USP28 protein and mRNA.
source: Notably, shRNA-mediated knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of KRAS led to reduced levels of USP28 protein (Figure 4E) and mRNA (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4E and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4F.

claim: The USP28 promoter contains two putative binding sites for the transcription factor cJUN.
source: To gain insight into the basis of KRAS-mediated regulation of USP28 transcription, we performed bioinformatic analysis on the USP28 promoter and identified two putative binding sites for the transcription factor cJUN (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: KRAS increases cJUN activity.
source: Notably, previous studies have shown that KRAS increases cJUN activity (Mechta et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mechta et al., 1997.

claim: In DLD-1 cells, cJUN was bound to the USP28 promoter.
source: The ChIP results of Figure 4G show, consistent with the bioinformatic prediction, that in DLD-1 cells cJUN was bound to the USP28 promoter.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Knockdown of cJUN resulted in decreased expression of USP28 and derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A.
source: Moreover, knockdown of cJUN (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) resulted in decreased expression of USP28 (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) and derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 4H and 4I.

claim: cJUN is responsible, at least in part, for RAS-mediated transcriptional upregulation of USP28.
source: Thus, cJUN is responsible, at least in part, for RAS-mediated transcriptional upregulation of USP28.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing cJUN binding to the USP28 promoter and effects of cJUN knockdown.

claim: USP28 contains two predicted phosphorylation sites for PRKD1.
source: Notably, USP28 contains two predicted phosphorylation sites for PRKD1 (consensus sequence LxRxxS, [Nishikawa et al., 1997]; Figure 5A), a serine/threonine protein kinase (Johannes et al., 1994) isolated in our RNAi screen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) that is dysregulated in a variety of cancers (Sundram et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 5A and citations to Nishikawa et al., 1997 and Johannes et al., 1994.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of PRKD1 in DLD-1 cells resulted in decreased ZNF304 protein levels, whereas ZNF304 mRNA levels were not significantly affected.
source: shRNA-mediated knockdown of PRKD1 in DLD-1 cells resulted in decreased ZNF304 protein levels (Figure 5B), whereas ZNF304 mRNA levels were not significantly affected (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5B and qRT-PCR data in Figure 5C.

claim: Treatment of DLD-1 cells with the PRKD1 chemical inhibitor CRT0066101 resulted in decreased ZNF304 protein levels, derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A, and loss of ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 binding to the three promoters.
source: Furthermore, treatment of DLD-1 cells with a PRKD1 chemical inhibitor, CRT0066101 (Harikumar et al., 2010), also resulted in decreased ZNF304 protein levels (Figure 5D), derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A (Figure 5E), and loss of ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 binding to the three promoters (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5D, qRT-PCR data in Figure 5E, and ChIP data in Figure 5F.

claim: PRKD1 protein and mRNA levels decreased following shRNA-mediated knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of KRAS.
source: Similar to the results with USP28, PRKD1 protein and mRNA levels decreased following shRNA-mediated knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of KRAS (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5G and qRT-PCR data in Figure 5H.

claim: USP28 and PRKD1 were stably associated.
source: Consistent with this possibility, we found that USP28 and PRKD1 were stably associated in a co-immunoprecipitation assay (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: PRKD1 could phosphorylate a USP28 peptide containing the second, more conserved predicted phosphorylation site.
source: Figure 5J shows that PRKD1 could phosphorylate a USP28 peptide containing the second, more conserved predicted phosphorylation site (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Unlike wild-type USP28, a USP28 derivative containing a mutation in the PRKD1 phosphorylation site, USP28(S899A), was unable to reduce ZNF304 ubiquitination.
source: Notably, unlike wild-type USP28, a USP28 derivative containing a mutation in the PRKD1 phosphorylation site, USP28(S899A), was unable to reduce ZNF304 ubiquitination (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by HA-ubiquitination pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Treatment with the PRKD1 inhibitor CRT0066101 prevented USP28 from reducing ubiquitination of ZNF304.
source: Likewise, treatment with the PRKD1 inhibitor CRT0066101 prevented USP28 from reducing ubiquitination of ZNF304 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by HA-ubiquitination pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The PRKD1 promoter contains consensus binding sites for the intestine-specific transcription factor CDX1.
source: To gain mechanistic insight into this process, we performed bioinformatic analysis on the PRKD1 promoter and identified consensus binding sites for the intestine-specific transcription factor CDX1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: KRAS positively regulates CDX1 activity through the mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway.
source: Notably, previous studies have shown that KRAS positively regulates CDX1 activity through the mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway (Lorentz et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lorentz et al., 1999.

claim: CDX1 was bound to the PRKD1 promoter in DLD-1 cells.
source: The ChIP results of Figure 5L show, consistent with the bioinformatic prediction, that CDX1 was bound to the PRKD1 promoter in DLD-1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Knockdown of CDX1 resulted in decreased expression of PRKD1 and derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A.
source: Moreover, knockdown of CDX1 (Figure 5–figure supplement 4A) resulted in decreased expression of PRKD1 (Figure 5M, Figure 5—figure supplement 4B) and derepression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A (Figure 5N, Figure 5—figure supplement 4C)
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 5M and 5N.

claim: CDX1 is responsible, at least in part, for RAS-mediated transcriptional upregulation of PRKD1.
source: Thus, CDX1 is responsible, at least in part, for RAS-mediated transcriptional upregulation of PRKD1.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing CDX1 binding to the PRKD1 promoter and effects of CDX1 knockdown.

claim: Approximately 70% of CRCs containing activated KRAS are CIMP-positive as defined by aberrant hypermethylation of a representative panel of ∼50 CIMP marker genes.
source: As stated above, approximately 70% of CRCs containing activated KRAS are CIMP-positive as defined by aberrant hypermethylation of a representative panel of ∼50 CIMP marker genes (Yagi et al., 2010; Kaneda and Yagi, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yagi et al., 2010 and Kaneda and Yagi, 2011.

claim: Knockdown of either KRAS or ZNF304 derepressed expression of all 50 CIMP marker genes analyzed.
source: Remarkably, knockdown of either KRAS or ZNF304 derepressed expression of all 50 CIMP marker genes analyzed (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Knockdown of either KRAS or ZNF304 derepressed VIM and SEPT9.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of either KRAS or ZNF304 also derepressed VIM and SEPT9 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), whose DNA hypermethylation is used to diagnose CRC (Gyparaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of KRAS or ZNF304 decreased promoter hypermethylation of a representative subset of CIMP marker genes.
source: Bisulfite sequencing analysis of a representative subset of CIMP marker genes, which included p14ARF, p16INK4A and seven additional genes, revealed that shRNA-mediated knockdown of KRAS or ZNF304 also decreased promoter hypermethylation (Figure 2E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: ChIP analysis showed significant enrichment of ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 on the promoters of nine CIMP marker genes.
source: ChIP analysis showed significant enrichment of ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 on the promoters of the nine CIMP marker genes (Figures 2D and 6B)
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figures 2D and 6B.

claim: Expression of nine CIMP marker genes was derepressed by the knockdown of the ZNF304 corepressors.
source: ChIP analysis showed significant enrichment of ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 on the promoters of the nine CIMP marker genes (Figures 2D and 6B), whose expression was also derepressed by the knockdown of the ZNF304 corepressors (Figures 2C and 6C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 2C and 6C.

claim: In CIMP-positive HCT116 and HCT15 CRC cells, ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 were associated with the promoters of nine CIMP marker genes.
source: In CIMP-positive HCT116 and HCT15 CRC cells (Zheng et al., 2000; Figure 6—figure supplement 3), ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 were associated with the promoters of the nine CIMP marker genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Expression of nine CIMP marker genes was derepressed by shRNA-mediated knockdown of ZNF304 or KRAS in HCT116 and HCT15 cells.
source: In CIMP-positive HCT116 and HCT15 CRC cells (Zheng et al., 2000; Figure 6—figure supplement 3), ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 were associated with the promoters of the nine CIMP marker genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 4), whose expression was derepressed by shRNA-mediated knockdown of ZNF304 or KRAS (Figures 2A and 3A, Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 2A, 3A, and Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: ZNF304 was substantially enriched at the promoters of nine CIMP marker genes in KRAS-positive human CRC tumors relative to matched normal colon.
source: The PAT-ChIP results of Figures 3I and 6D show that ZNF304 was substantially enriched at the promoters of the nine CIMP marker genes in KRAS-positive human CRC tumors relative to matched normal colon.
evidence: This is supported by PAT-ChIP data shown in Figures 3I and 6D.

claim: Bisulfite sequencing analysis confirmed promoter hypermethylation of representative CIMP marker genes in all KRAS-positive CRC tumor samples.
source: Bisulfite sequencing analysis of representative CIMP marker genes confirmed promoter hypermethylation in all KRAS-positive CRC tumor samples (Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6.

claim: In undifferentiated H9 hESCs, ZNF304 was present at high levels, which markedly decreased following differentiation by retinoic acid treatment.
source: The immunoblot results of Figure 7A show that in undifferentiated H9 hESCs, ZNF304 was present at high levels, which markedly decreased following differentiation by retinoic acid treatment.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In undifferentiated H9 hESCs, ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 were substantially enriched at the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters, which was largely lost following differentiation.
source: Moreover, in undifferentiated H9 hESCs ZNF304, KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 were substantially enriched at the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters (Figure 7B), which was largely lost following differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Knockdown of ZNF304 in undifferentiated H9 hESCs resulted in decreased association of KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 with the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters and increased expression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A.
source: Finally, knockdown of ZNF304 in undifferentiated H9 hESCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) resulted in decreased association of KAP1, SETDB1, and DNMT1 with the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters (Figure 7C) and increased expression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 7C and qRT-PCR data in Figure 7D.

claim: In H9 hESCs, the p14ARF and p16INK4A promoters were not hypermethylated, unlike in DLD-1 cells.
source: However, the bisulfite sequencing results of Figure 7E show that unlike DLD-1 cells, in H9 hESCs the p14ARF and p16INK4A promoters were not hypermethylated.
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: There was substantial enrichment of H3K27me3 at the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters in H9 hESCs, whereas in DLD-1 cells the level of H3K27me3 was substantially lower.
source: The ChIP results of Figure 7F show substantial enrichment of H3K27me3 at the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters in H9 hESCs, whereas in DLD-1 cells the level of H3K27me3 was substantially lower.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The level of H3K9me3 at the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters was much higher in DLD-1 cells than in H9 hESCs.
source: By contrast, the level of histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) at the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters was much higher in DLD-1 cells than in H9 hESCs.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: There was no significant enrichment of H3K4me3 at the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters in either DLD-1 cells or H9 hESCs.
source: As expected, there was no significant enrichment of histone H3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3), a mark associated with transcription activity, in either DLD-1 cells or H9 hESCs.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: In both H9 hESCs and DLD-1 cells, the PRC2 subunit EZH2 and the PRC1 subunit BMI1 were associated with the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters.
source: The results of Figure 7G show that in both H9 hESCs and DLD-1 cells, the PRC2 subunit EZH2 and the PRC1 subunit BMI1 were associated with the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: In both H9 hESCs and DLD-1 cells, knockdown of ZNF304 decreased binding of EZH2 and BMI1 to the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters.
source: Figure 7H shows that in both H9 hESCs and DLD-1 cells, knockdown of ZNF304 decreased binding of EZH2 and BMI1 to the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters, which, as expected, was accompanied by a loss of H3K27me3 (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: In both H9 hESCs and DLD-1 cells, knockdown of ZNF304 resulted in decreased H3K9me3 and increased H3K4me3 at the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters.
source: Also, as expected, in both H9 hESCs and DLD-1 cells, the knockdown of ZNF304 resulted in decreased H3K9me3 and increased H3K4me3 at the p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A promoters (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Knockdown of EZH2 or BMI1 increased expression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A in H9 hESCs but not in DLD-1 cells.
source: Consistent with this idea, the knockdown of EZH2 or BMI1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B) increased expression of p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4A in H9 hESCs but not in DLD-1 cells (Figure 7J, Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: In a previous study, silencing of the Fas tumor suppressor in RAS-transformed NIH 3T3 cells requires ZFP354B, which like ZNF304 is a KRAB-ZFP protein.
source: In a previous study, we have found that silencing of the Fas tumor suppressor in RAS-transformed NIH 3T3 cells requires ZFP354B (Gazin et al., 2007), which like ZNF304 is a KRAB-ZFP protein.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gazin et al., 2007.

claim: Like ZNF304, ZFP354B levels are increased by activated RAS.
source: Moreover, like ZNF304, ZFP354B levels are increased by activated RAS.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: Expression of activated KRAS(G12V) in non-transformed WI-38 fibroblasts transcriptionally activated p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4.
source: Consistent with this idea, we found, as expected, that expression of activated KRAS(G12V) in non-transformed WI-38 fibroblasts transcriptionally activated p14ARF, p15INK4B, and p16INK4 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In WI-38 cells, KRAS failed to increase ZNF304 protein levels.
source: However, in contrast to the results in KRAS-positive CRC cell lines, in WI-38 cells KRAS failed to increase ZNF304 protein levels (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In WI-38 cells, KRAS did not significantly stimulate USP28 and PRKD1 transcription.
source: However, in contrast to the results in KRAS-positive CRC cell lines, in WI-38 cells KRAS failed to increase ZNF304 protein levels (Figure 8B) or significantly stimulate USP28 and PRKD1 transcription (Figure 8C)
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8C.
